hypothesis: French beach enforcement displaces launch sites along the coast and into inland waterways
mechanism: More police, surveillance and destruction of equipment at known beaches raise the cost of launching there, so organisers move launches to less-watched beaches, rivers and canals, or use taxi boats.
supporting_evidence: Home Affairs Committee (2022): launches moved further from the ports in 2021 as gangs evaded enforcement. The Border Security Commander (2026) reports signs of displacement further south and into Belgium. The Commons Library (2026) links taxi boats to better equipment detection at known departure points. The French inquiry and its officials describe a 'cascade' of displacement. Oxford cites 2022-23 reports of departures from further along the coast and inland. The NCA and Border Forensics make the same link. MMC finds departure choice varies with police presence.
contradicting_evidence: Launches were already spread along 100+ km of coast in 2021 (HAC para 37). MMC says choice also depends on nationality and network. The prevented share of attempts stayed around 35-47% from 2018 to 2025 rather than rising. No systematic launch-site series exists to show a change in distribution over time.
missing_evidence: Annual counts of launch attempts by coastal sector (French prefecture/CROSS data), before and after specific deployments. Coordinates of taxi-boat launch and pickup points. Any published UK-France evaluation.
alternative_explanations: Organiser choice driven by nationality-based territory and network control (GI-TOC, MMC). Changes in reporting attention. Weather windows varying along the coast.
confidence_rationale: Consistent qualitative accounts from official, parliamentary, NGO and research sources, but all descriptive or attributed. No spatial time series was located.

hypothesis: France's 2025-26 at-sea interception doctrine for taxi boats changes launch tactics or geography
mechanism: At-sea stops of taxi boats before (or, reportedly, after) boarding remove the method's advantage in shallow water, so organisers relocate launches (for example to Belgium) or change pickup practices.
supporting_evidence: The doctrine was announced on 28 November 2025. The first interception was on 17 January 2026 at Gravelines; the first seven interceptions led to 73 people in custody. Belgian launch attempts rose to 32 in January-April 2026 from 2 in 2025. The BSC frames Belgian launches as a response to French enforcement. The Dunkirk prosecutor speculated that intercepted boats carried migrants because they had launched from Belgium.
contradicting_evidence: The doctrine is a handful of months old and only a few interceptions are documented. The French regional prefect attributes the early-2026 fall mainly to weather, and the Police aux frontières to the international context and less pressure at the Franco-Italian border. Belgian launches reportedly still collect passengers in French waters.
missing_evidence: Count of at-sea interventions by month and location. Launch-origin data for 2026. A before/after comparison controlling for weather.
alternative_explanations: Weather (fewer windows in early 2026). Lower upstream migration pressure. Seasonal timing. The broader April 2026 funding deal and CRS deployment.
confidence_rationale: Too recent: mostly announcements and single events. Timing coincides with several other changes.

hypothesis: UK-funded French prevention (Sandhurst 2018, the 2023 Declaration, the 2026 deal) reduces arrivals
mechanism: More personnel, surveillance and interception prevent a share of attempts and, over time, deter attempts.
supporting_evidence: About a third to nearly half of recorded attempts are prevented. The BSC reports over 20,000 preventions in 2025/26. 2023 arrivals fell 36% after the March 2023 Declaration. First-half 2026 arrivals are well below 2025.
contradicting_evidence: The Home Office attributes most of the 2023 fall to a 93% drop in Albanians. Arrivals rose again in 2024 and 2025. The prevented share did not rise after 2023 (35% in 2025). The ICIBI found evidence for the port-security effect inconclusive. The BSC says changes cannot be attributed to any single intervention. Effectiveness reviews are not published.
missing_evidence: Published UK-France evaluation metrics. Unique-person attempt data. A counterfactual analysis controlling for weather and upstream flows.
alternative_explanations: Nationality-specific returns (Albania). Weather. Upstream EU migration flows. Organised crime adapting by overloading to keep arrivals up.
confidence_rationale: Prevention volumes are documented, but no evidence isolates an effect on arrivals, and official sources themselves decline to attribute.

hypothesis: UK deterrence policy (Illegal Migration Act 2023, Rwanda, the 2025 returns pilot) reduces crossings
mechanism: Lower expected benefit of arrival (no protection, removal to a third country or France) reduces demand for crossings.
supporting_evidence: Wood (2025) reports return agreements associated with fewer arrivals on viable days (abstract only). The BSC reports 'emerging' evidence of deterrence among migrants in France. The Home Office's impact assessment cites a stronger evidence base for effects on choice of destination.
contradicting_evidence: No one was forcibly relocated to Rwanda; the scheme was cancelled and most IMA provisions were repealed. The returns pilot returned 1,087 people in 11 months (about 1% of August-December 2025 arrivals). The impact assessment cites an academic consensus of little to no evidence that destination policy deters. The Home Office-commissioned review found insufficient evidence that restrictive UK asylum policy affects numbers. The Home Office Permanent Secretary could not conclude Rwanda would deter enough.
missing_evidence: Wood's full model and return-agreement coding. Evaluation of the returns pilot. Arrival changes by nationality in scope of the pilot.
alternative_explanations: Weather. Nationality mix. French prevention. Upstream flows.
confidence_rationale: Several policies never operated at scale, and official appraisals and reviews found insufficient evidence of deterrence. One peer-reviewed abstract suggests a return-agreement association.

hypothesis: NCA/BSC upstream disruption and equipment seizures constrain boat supply, raising occupancy rather than reducing arrivals
mechanism: Seizing boats, engines and suppliers makes equipment scarcer and costlier, so organisers load more people per available boat and deliver equipment just in time.
supporting_evidence: The BSC says organisers make the most of scarce supplies by overloading, and use just-in-time delivery. Border Forensics says supply disruption led to larger, lower-quality, overcrowded inflatables. The Commons Library reports overcrowding attributed to supply restriction and cost. The NCA says groups increased people per boat as boat events fell 3% in 2025. Boats fell 39% from 2022 to 2025 while people fell 9%.
contradicting_evidence: GI-TOC and French border police attribute overloading to profit-seeking and poorer clients rather than scarcity. The BSC's claim that seizures potentially stopped up to 33,000 attempts is unexplained. Occupancy was already rising in 2019-2021, before the scale-up of upstream disruption.
missing_evidence: Time series of seizures against boat availability or price at the coast. Evidence that loads rose after specific supply shocks, such as the arrest of a major boat supplier.
alternative_explanations: Client profile and price (H13). Enforcement at launch favouring fewer, bigger loads (H06). Larger boats (H09).
confidence_rationale: Several independent accounts propose the mechanism, but all are attributed. No supply-side data link seizures to occupancy.

hypothesis: Launch tactics (taxi boats, simultaneous launches, overloading) are organised-crime adaptations that raise occupancy and change pickup geography
mechanism: Fewer, fuller launches and multiple simultaneous launches overwhelm limited police capacity at the beach. Taxi boats avoid beach checks by picking up people already in the water.
supporting_evidence: The BSC lists simultaneous launches, diversions, overloading and taxi boats. The Commons Library reports a taxi-boat success rate estimated at over 80%. The NCA's 2026 assessment names the taxi-boat method as a capability driver. Home Office data show fewer very large arrival days and more boats with 70+ people.
contradicting_evidence: No prevalence series for taxi boats or simultaneous launches. The 80% figure is second-hand and undefined. Occupancy growth predates widespread reports of taxi boats (2019-2022).
missing_evidence: Share of launches by method per year. French data on taxi-boat interceptions and pickups.
alternative_explanations: Supply constraint (H05). Client price and profile (H13). Larger boats (H09).
confidence_rationale: Tactics are consistently reported by official sources, but their contribution to occupancy or geography is not quantified.

hypothesis: Weather and sea conditions drive short-term and seasonal variation in arrivals
mechanism: Low waves, favourable wind and calm surf open crossing windows; arrivals concentrate on viable days and in late summer.
supporting_evidence: Red days are 35% of days but carry 84% of arrivals (May 2021-April 2025). Wood (2025) quantifies the effects of waves, sea temperature and wind on day viability (abstract). The Home Office says fluctuations are often due to weather. The Hauts-de-France prefect attributes the early-2026 fall mainly to weather. A minister cited benign weather for the late-2024 rise. The Home Affairs Committee cites calmer weather in 2021.
contradicting_evidence: Red days are not pure weather: they include recent crossing trends, and baselines were re-set in April 2023. Arrivals per red day ranged from 212 to 441, and the year to April 2023 had the fewest red days but the most arrivals. The Migration Observatory doubts that weather explains long-term increases.
missing_evidence: An exogenous weather-only index (for example wave height and wind from reanalysis) regressed on daily launches and attempts, not just arrivals. Wood's full results.
alternative_explanations: Supply and demand shocks (Albania 2022, Horn of Africa 2025). Enforcement intensity varying by season. Reporting and detection changes.
confidence_rationale: Direct official and peer-reviewed support for the day-to-day and seasonal contribution. This confidence does NOT extend to multi-year trends or geography, where the evidence is weak and the red-day measure is endogenous.

hypothesis: Tides and tidal currents shape launch timing and location
mechanism: Tidal state affects beach access, shallow-water pickups and drift, favouring certain times and places.
supporting_evidence: The Home Affairs Committee notes strong tides in the Strait (context only). The Commons Library notes that strong sea currents were believed to deter Belgian departures.
contradicting_evidence: No source located that tests tides against crossings. The Home Office's red-day inputs listed do not include tide.
missing_evidence: Any analysis of launch or arrival times against tidal state, or French operational data on tidal timing.
confidence_rationale: No direct evidence located; noted as a gap, not disproved.

hypothesis: Larger boats (increased vessel capacity) explain rising people per boat
mechanism: Organisers source longer, higher-payload inflatables, so each launch carries more people.
supporting_evidence: The NCA (2021) reported inflatables up to 10 m. Oxford says more people per boat 'reflects the use of larger boats'. Border Forensics says facilitators sourced larger inflatables. Boats with 70+ people rose from 18 to 202 between the two-year periods.
contradicting_evidence: GI-TOC says bigger boats explain rising loads only 'in some sense' and that 'in the majority of cases' boats are simply packed with more people. Oxford adds that boats may be used beyond capacity. The BSC and the Commons Library emphasise overloading. French border police link higher loads to poorer clients. Occupancy measures people on arrival, not rated capacity.
missing_evidence: Representative data on length, beam and rated payload by year (vessel workstream). Loads relative to rated capacity.
alternative_explanations: Overloading of similar boats (H05, H06, H13). A change in how boats are counted or reconciled.
confidence_rationale: Larger craft appearing is reported, but the main sources attribute much of the occupancy rise to loading density, and no representative dimension series exists.

hypothesis: Larger boats enable longer routes (project hypothesis H2)
mechanism: Greater size or payload is assumed to bring more fuel and range, allowing launches further from Dover.
supporting_evidence: Departures now occur along a wider coastline (Berck to Belgium) and from Belgium in 2026. Oxford says some journeys 'may have become longer'.
contradicting_evidence: Every source that explains wider launch geography attributes it to enforcement displacement, not vessel capability. Belgian taxi boats reportedly return to French waters to load, so the loaded passage need not be longer. Informants saw Belgian crossings as riskier because they are longer. Border Forensics finds deaths shifting closer to French shores. Overloading reduces freeboard and safety margins and would reduce, not extend, safe range. No engine, fuel or range dataset exists.
missing_evidence: Documented origin and destination pairs with tracks. Fuel carried and engine power by year. Rated range. Where interceptions and rescues occur relative to launch sites.
alternative_explanations: Enforcement displacement (H01, H02). Taxi-boat pickup geography (H06). Reporting of rare outliers.
confidence_rationale: No direct support; the displacement explanation accounts for the geographic observations; the evidence reviewed runs against the proposed causal link.

hypothesis: Changes in propulsion or fuel availability alter crossing patterns
mechanism: More powerful or additional engines, or more fuel, change speed and range; fuel scarcity at the coast constrains launches.
supporting_evidence: The French inquiry describes boats of about ten metres with one or two low-powered outboard engines (a description, not a trend). The BSC mentions just-in-time equipment delivery.
contradicting_evidence: No longitudinal engine-power or fuel dataset was found. 'Low-powered' engines argue against a propulsion-driven range increase.
missing_evidence: Seizure and inspection records of engines and fuel by year, with sampling caveats (vessel workstream). MAIB fuel observations.
confidence_rationale: No evidence of change was located; this is an evidence gap, not a disproof.

hypothesis: Organised-crime professionalisation and market dynamics sustain crossings despite enforcement
mechanism: Loose, low-barrier smuggling networks with replaceable members respond to enforcement by adapting routes, prices and tactics. Competition lowers prices and expands the market.
supporting_evidence: Oxford (loose networks, low barriers), GI-TOC (industrialisation, Kurdish control, recruitment campaigns), MMC (adaptive and professionalised), the Channel Crossings project and Border Forensics (enforcement strengthens professional smugglers), and the BSC (facilitators readily replaceable). Price estimates fell from about €14,000 (2018) to about €1,500-4,000 by 2024-2026. The ICIBI in 2020 said the threat was adept at responding to checks.
contradicting_evidence: Price data are uncertain and vary by nationality. The Commons Library reports evidence of facilitators losing control in 2024. The 2023 arrivals fall shows networks do not fully offset shocks (for example Albania).
missing_evidence: Systematic price series. Network disruption outcomes over time.
confidence_rationale: Broad agreement across official, NGO and academic sources, but the evidence is qualitative and much of it attributed.

hypothesis: Demand and push factors (conflict, nationality mix, upstream EU flows) drive volumes, and client profile affects occupancy
mechanism: The number and origin of people reaching northern France sets the pool of potential crossers. Poorer client groups pay less, so organisers load more people per boat.
supporting_evidence: Large nationality shifts in the year to June 2026 (Somali +76%, Sudanese +11%, Afghan -37%). The 2023 fall is largely an Albanian drop. The NCA cites Horn of Africa demand. French border police link Eritrean and Sudanese clients paying €1,500-2,000 to more passengers. The Police aux frontières links the 2026 fall to less pressure at the Franco-Italian border. Wood's abstract reports past EU irregular immigration as a significant factor. The Home Office review finds networks and protection elsewhere shape destination.
contradicting_evidence: Demand does not explain the timing of the 2018 route switch (H14) or daily variation (H07). Nationality-level asylum grant rates changed without clear crossing responses (not tested here).
missing_evidence: Upstream arrival series (Frontex, Italy) set against Channel attempts with lags. Price data by nationality.
confidence_rationale: Official nationality statistics are strong, but causal links rest on attributed assessments and one abstract.

hypothesis: Route substitution: securing lorries, ports and the tunnel displaced irregular entry into small boats (2018-2020), with some reverse substitution possible
mechanism: Fortifying Calais, Coquelles and Dunkirk, together with Brexit and COVID freight disruption, raised the cost and risk of clandestine lorry entry, making boats comparatively cheaper and more reliable.
supporting_evidence: Detected in-country and port detections fell (7,257 and 1,052 in 2018; 1,816 and 204 in 2025) as boats rose. French land-route interceptions fell from 57,137 (2016) to 3,217 (2025). The Home Affairs Committee, French inquiry, Oxford, IPPR, the Channel Crossings project and peer-reviewed papers (JEMS 2024, ERS 2021, PQ 2024) all describe the shift. GI-TOC reports boat passage became far cheaper than trucks. Getlink reports lorry attempts rising again when sea conditions were poor in winter 2025-26.
contradicting_evidence: The ICIBI (2020) judged the port-security explanation 'inconclusive'; lorry-drop encounters rose by a third in 2019, and the Calais trend was confounded by the 2016 camp clearance. The Home Office warns that detection varies by method and attributes the 2020 decline partly to COVID. The Channel Crossings project suggests greater visibility may mean more people are counted rather than more people crossing.
missing_evidence: Estimates of undetected clandestine entry. Unique-person data across methods. A pre-2018 small-boat baseline.
alternative_explanations: Growth in demand. COVID freight collapse. Brexit (end of Dublin). Differential detection.
confidence_rationale: Strong, convergent descriptive and official-statistical evidence of a shift in detected methods, but an independent inspectorate called the causal evidence inconclusive and detection differs by method.

hypothesis: Measurement and detection artefacts explain part of the apparent change
mechanism: Arrivals-based occupancy misses people prevented, rescued or returned. Small boats are far more detectable than lorry entry. Prevention definitions shift. Official sources disagree on units.
supporting_evidence: The Home Office says not to compare methods and that small boats are the most likely to be detected. Border Forensics argues occupancy on arrival underestimates departure density. The French inquiry's 2025 attempt figures conflict (63,899 vs 22,427). The Home Affairs Committee's 2021 prevention figures conflict (19,000 vs 23,000+). Unreconciled events are excluded from the Home Office boat bands.
contradicting_evidence: Occupancy and boat counts come from the same administrative system over time, so the direction of the 2018-2026 occupancy rise is unlikely to be an artefact (DEFINITION-ARRIVALS; the ANNUAL and OCCUPANCY claims).
missing_evidence: Documentation of reconciliation rules over time. Departure-side counts of people per boat from French rescues.
confidence_rationale: Documented caveats and inconsistencies are real; they qualify magnitudes and cross-method comparisons, not the direction of the occupancy trend.

hypothesis: Search and rescue acts as a 'pull factor' for Channel crossings
mechanism: Expected rescue lowers perceived risk, encouraging attempts or riskier loading.
supporting_evidence: No Channel-specific evidence located. The idea is raised in French and UK debate, as recorded by the French inquiry.
contradicting_evidence: A peer-reviewed Central Mediterranean study (2011-2020) found no discernible effect of rescue periods on attempts, while pushbacks did affect flows. The French inquiry cites that study and 2001-02 Sangatte survey evidence that most migrants were unaware of reception facilities beforehand.
missing_evidence: Any Channel test, for example rescue capacity changes set against attempts.
confidence_rationale: Only indirect evidence from another route, which contradicts the hypothesis. Transferability is untested.
